sections.html:
Montclair does not ask sellers for a fresh certificate of occupancy, but it does insist that every permit and violation on the property be closed out before the deed changes hands. Add a median home value above $900,000 and a tax bill driven mostly by the school district, and the sale has a few features you will not find in every Essex County town.

The typical owner-occupied home is worth $906,400, and 56.9 percent of households own. Typical gross rent is $2,063 and median household income is $151,075. Population is about 44,633, up from 40,921 in 2020. Low turnover is part of the picture, since 86.2 percent of residents stayed in the same house through the prior year. That means a listing is measured against very few comparable sales, so a well-prepared house can set its own price level while a house with open permits gets marked down quickly.

Montclair climbs the eastern slope of First Mountain, and higher streets look toward Manhattan about 12 miles away. Named areas include Upper Montclair, Watchung Plaza, Church Street, Frog Hollow and South End, split between ZIP Codes 07042 and 07043. Several brooks drain east, so a wet basement is a common buyer question.

Seven NJ Transit rail stops on the Montclair-Boonton Line serve the township: Bay Street, Walnut Street, Watchung Avenue, Upper Montclair, Mountain Avenue, Montclair Heights and Montclair State University. Trains go to New York Penn Station and Hoboken. Bus routes 11, 28, 29, 34, 97, 191 and 705 mostly follow Bloomfield Avenue. Listings tend to name the elementary school zone alongside the station, because buyers ask about both.

sections.h2: Closing without a new certificate of occupancy
sections.html:
A Building Department notice from June 2025 says the township does not require a new certificate of occupancy as a condition of selling, mortgaging or refinancing. Instead, every current construction permit must be closed, and every open violation must be cleared, before closing.

Order the permit history first through an Open Public Records Act request. Then phone the department at 973-509-4951 to schedule the closeouts. The office sits on the second floor of the Municipal Building at 205 Claremont Avenue and keeps Monday to Friday counter hours between 8:30 and 4:30.

  • A finished basement, new deck or swapped boiler without a final inspection is the usual culprit.
  • A second kitchen needs evidence that it was permitted, such as a closed permit.
  • Landlords with tenants should ask the township's Rent Control Office what applies to a rental building.

Montclair bills in four installments, and the township gives a ten-day grace window. Arrears up to $1,500 carry 8% interest and the excess carries 18%.

Montclair tax installment due dates.
InstallmentDue date
FirstFebruary 1
SecondMay 1
ThirdAugust 1
FourthNovember 1

By share of the whole levy, schools take 54.25%, the township 23.72%, Essex County 14.53%, the Type I district 2.90%, a voter-approved school referendum 2.32%, the library 1.57% and open space 0.71%. Because the school share dominates, a buyer's monthly cost can change by more than the township's own budget would suggest. Have the latest quarterly amount ready, since your closing attorney will prorate the quarter underway.

Challenge the assessed value with the Essex County Board of Taxation. The appeal must be received before May 1, and a dissatisfied owner may then go to the New Jersey Tax Court within 45 days of the Board's notice.

The tax rate itself is not appealable under state law, only the value it is applied to. Montclair also auctions tax sale certificates, generally once each year, and the winning bidder buys a lien, not the house. Clear any unpaid municipal, water or sewer balance before you sign a contract.

sections.h2: Deed recording and the state transfer charge
sections.html:
The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages records Montclair deeds. The office covers all 22 county municipalities, and an attorney or title agent usually files yours.

With values this high, the state's graduated fee matters. For deeds submitted on or after July 10, 2025, a sale over $1 million carries a percentage of the full price: 1% up to $2 million, 2% up to $2.5 million, 2.5% up to $3 million, 3% up to $3.5 million and 3.5% beyond. The law shifted the charge to the seller, so build it into your net proceeds before you accept an offer close to a threshold.

sections.h2: Agent, owner sale or cash buyer?
sections.html:
A listing usually earns the top price in a market with this much demand, provided permits are closed and the house is staged. A direct buyer who pays cash and accepts the house as it stands makes sense when permits are unfinished, an estate needs settling, or tenants complicate showings.

  • Agent listing: widest exposure and strongest price, with preparation and showings on your side.
  • Owner sale: you keep the commission but also take on pricing, disclosures and negotiation.
  • Cash buyer: condition is not an obstacle and the date is flexible, at a price set below a polished listing.

Line up the net from each route after payoffs, taxes and permit closeouts, then decide. A cash quote costs nothing to request and carries no obligation.

Start with the paper trail. File the Open Public Records Act request for the permit history, and compare it with what you know about the house, including any finished basement, deck, boiler replacement or second kitchen. Each gap is a closeout to schedule with the Building Department.

Next, gather the money figures: the latest quarterly tax amount, any unpaid municipal, water or sewer balance, and the mortgage payoff. Your closing attorney will need them to prorate the quarter underway and to draw the statement. If your price is near one of the thresholds above $1 million, ask the attorney to run the graduated fee at your contract price before you accept.

Allow time on both ends. Building Department inspections have to be scheduled by phone, and the counter is open only on weekdays during set hours, so a closeout can take several visits if the work was never inspected. Tell your attorney early which items are open, and avoid promising a closing date that depends on an inspection you have not yet booked so the contract date reflects reality. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and can close on the day you choose, but the permit and violation closeouts still have to happen, so ask the buyer who handles them.

faqs.q: Will Montclair demand a new certificate of occupancy before my closing?
faqs.a: No. The Building Department's June 2025 notice states that a new certificate is not a condition of a sale, mortgage or refinance. Open permits and violations still have to be closed before closing.

faqs.q: Which dates does Montclair use for tax installments?
faqs.a: Installments fall on the first of February, May, August and November, with ten days of grace. Late arrears up to $1,500 accrue 8% and amounts above that accrue 18%.

faqs.q: Which office files a Montclair deed?
faqs.a: The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages. It records transactions for all 22 municipalities in the county, and closing attorneys or title agents normally submit the paperwork.

faqs.q: Can an unfinished permit hold up a Montclair closing?
faqs.a: Yes. Any current construction permit must be closed first. Request the permit history under the Open Public Records Act, then call the Building Department at 973-509-4951 to arrange inspections or closeout.

faqs.q: By when must a Montclair assessment appeal be filed?
faqs.a: The appeal must reach the Essex County Board of Taxation before May 1. A further appeal to the New Jersey Tax Court must be filed within 45 days of the Board's notice.
